title: Fresh rectal bleeding in a 75-year-old man: consent and rectal examination
desc: This station involves a focused history from a 75-year-old accountant in the ED who passed painless dark red blood with clots a few hours ago, followed by consent for and a rectal examination. The candidate then interprets his observations, blood results and a colonoscopy report. They give the diagnosis and differentials, outline management in the emergency department, explain the findings to David and safety-net.
focus: Acute painless rectal bleeding in an older man: consenting for and performing a rectal examination, risk-stratifying the bleed and recognising a diverticular bleed
stem:
You are a final-year medical student on placement in a metropolitan Emergency Department. David Hughes, a 75-year-old accountant, has come in after passing blood from his back passage a few hours ago. The triage note records type 2 diabetes and chronic constipation, treated with metformin and regular Movicol, and no known allergies. His last faecal occult blood test (FOBT) 2 years ago was negative, and he has no family history of cancer.

He has been triaged, has an IV cannula in and has had bloods sent. Your supervising registrar has asked you to assess him, including a rectal examination. A nurse is with you and will carry out any instructions you give.
tasks: Take a focused history from David and perform a focused examination, including consent for and a rectal examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you his observations, his blood results and a colonoscopy report. Interpret them, give your most likely diagnosis and differentials, then outline your management approach, explain the colonoscopy findings to David and safety-net (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are David Hughes, a 75-year-old accountant. You are sitting on the trolley in a hospital gown, comfortable and not in pain. You are polite and precise, as an accountant is, but you are embarrassed about the bleeding and a bit nervous about the "finger test". Give details only when you are asked. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they are examining. If there is no manikin, the candidate describes each step of the rectal examination and the examiner gives the findings.

Opening line: "I'm sorry to be a bother, but I passed a lot of blood from down below this morning and my wife made me come in."

The bleeding (give only when asked)

  • When: twice today. The first time was about 10:30 this morning at home. You felt a sudden urge to go and passed a soft motion followed by a lot of blood. The second time was about 12 o'clock, a bit less.
  • Amount: "The whole bowl went red. There were clots in it, maybe a cupful of blood the first time." Less the second time.
  • Colour: dark red, "like red wine", with clots. Mixed with the motion and in the bowl, not just a streak on the paper.
  • Pain: no pain at all, not in your tummy and not in your back passage. Opening your bowels did not hurt.
  • First time: you have never bled from the back passage before.
  • Effect: after the first episode you felt a little light-headed when you stood up from the toilet. It passed after you sat down for a minute. You did not faint or fall. No chest pain, no breathlessness, no palpitations.

Bowels and other symptoms (only when asked about each)

  • Bowel habit: you have been constipated for as long as you can remember. With one Movicol sachet a day you go every day or two and the motions are soft. This has not changed in years. You strain at times when you forget the Movicol.
  • No lump coming out of the back passage, no itch, no pain on opening the bowels, no mucus.
  • No diarrhoea, no vomiting, no fever. No recent travel and nobody sick at home. No new foods.
  • No black, tarry motions. No vomiting blood or coffee-ground material. No indigestion.
  • No tummy pain, now or in the past. No bloating that is new.
  • No weight loss (your weight is steady at about 82 kg), appetite normal, no unusual tiredness, no night sweats.

Background (only when asked; the triage note already gives the basics)

  • Past history: type 2 diabetes for about 10 years, "well controlled, my GP says". Chronic constipation. No previous bleeding, no liver disease, no heart disease or stroke. No operations on your tummy and no radiotherapy.
  • Bowel tests: you do the home poo test kits when they come in the post; the last one, 2 years ago, was clear. You have never had a colonoscopy.
  • Medications: metformin 1 g twice a day and Movicol one sachet a day. If asked specifically: no aspirin, no blood thinners (warfarin, apixaban, rivaroxaban, clopidogrel), no anti-inflammatories (ibuprofen, Nurofen, Voltaren), no fish oil or supplements.
  • Allergies: none to medicines. If asked about latex: "No, never had a problem with gloves."
  • Family history: no bowel cancer or other cancers, no bowel disease in the family.
  • Social: semi-retired accountant; you still do tax returns for long-standing clients from your desk at home. You live with your wife Margaret, who drove you in and is in the waiting room. Never smoked. A couple of beers on the weekend. Diet: "meat and three veg, not much fruit, I'm not one for salads." You don't do much exercise.

Ideas, concerns and expectations

  • Idea: "I wondered if it was piles from all the straining over the years."
  • Concern: you are worried it could be bowel cancer, "even though the poo test was clear". You are embarrassed about the examination.
  • Expectation: to find out what is causing it, and you hope to go home tonight because you have clients tomorrow.

Consent for the rectal examination

  • When the candidate explains the rectal examination, ask: "Will it hurt?" and "Do you really need to do it?"
  • If they explain clearly why it is needed, what will happen, that you can ask them to stop at any time, and offer a chaperone, agree: "All right, if it helps find out what's going on." You would like the nurse as the chaperone rather than your wife.
  • If they start without explaining or asking your permission, say: "Hang on, what exactly are you going to do?"
  • If asked whether your back passage is sore or you have any wounds or infection there: no.

The nurse and how David changes

  • If the candidate asks for observations, the nurse gives the triage set: RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air, BP 110/75, HR 65 regular, temperature 37.2 °C, alert, pain 0/10, BGL 8.1 mmol/L.
  • If asked to be the chaperone, the nurse stays in the room for the examination.
  • At the 8-minute mark, or as soon as the rectal examination is finished if that is earlier, the nurse says: "He's just passed about 100 mL of dark red blood with some small clots into a pan. He felt a bit light-headed sitting up for it." If the candidate asks for repeat observations: HR 76, BP 106/70, the rest unchanged. Lying down, David feels fine again.
  • If postural BP is requested after the further bleed, the nurse says he was light-headed sitting up; the examiner credits the request and gives the lying values only (BP 106/70, HR 76). Do not stand him.
  • If the candidate orders fluids, a group and hold or crossmatch, withholding metformin, or anything else, the nurse confirms she will arrange it, and the examiner says: "Noted. Please cover your management in Part 2."
  • If the candidate asks for blood results or imaging, the examiner says they will be given in Part 2.

Exam findings (give only when the candidate says what they are examining)

  • General: well and alert, comfortable, not in pain, not pale. Weight 82 kg.
  • Vital signs: BP 110/75, HR 65 regular, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.2 °C.
  • Postural BP (if asked before the further bleed): lying 110/75 with HR 65; standing 106/72 with HR 72. No dizziness on standing.
  • Perfusion and hydration: warm peripheries, CRT 2 seconds, moist mucous membranes. No conjunctival pallor.
  • Hands, face and skin: no stigmata of chronic liver disease. No telangiectasia.
  • Abdomen: not distended, no scars. Soft and non-tender throughout, no guarding. No masses. Liver and spleen not palpable. Normal bowel sounds. No hernias.
  • Rectal examination, inspection: perianal skin normal. No skin tags, fissures, external haemorrhoids, fistula openings or masses. No prolapse when he bears down. Dark red blood smeared at the anal margin.
  • Perianal sensation and anal reflex (give only if the candidate asks; not needed for this presentation): sensation intact to light touch; anal reflex present.
  • Digital examination: entry comfortable. Normal anal tone at rest and a good voluntary squeeze. Rectal wall smooth all the way round (posterior, both lateral walls, anterior). No mass, no tenderness, no stricture. Prostate smooth, symmetrically and mildly enlarged, median sulcus felt, not tender, no nodules.
  • Glove: soft brown stool mixed with dark red blood and small clots. No mucus. No black, tarry stool.
  • Heart and chest: dual heart sounds, no murmurs; chest clear.

check.x: Professionalism
Washes hands, introduces self and role (final-year medical student), confirms David's identity and gains consent for the consultation.
Acknowledges his embarrassment and worry, uses plain language ("back passage", not "PR"), keeps him covered with a sheet and explains each step before doing it.
History
Characterises the bleeding:

kids.x: Timing: twice today (about 10:30 and 12:00), never before
Volume and colour: the bowl went red, about a cupful, dark red with clots, mixed with the motion rather than a streak on the paper
Painless: no abdominal pain and no pain on opening the bowels

check.x: Asks about the effects of blood loss: light-headedness on standing (brief, after the first bleed), fainting or falls, chest pain, breathlessness or palpitations.
check.d: Score if light-headedness or fainting and at least one cardiorespiratory symptom are asked.

check.x: Screens for colorectal cancer: change in bowel habit (none in years), weight loss, tiredness, night sweats, and confirms the negative FOBT 2 years ago, no previous colonoscopy and no family history.
check.d: Score if at least 3 of the symptoms are asked, including change in bowel habit and weight loss.

check.x: Screens for anorectal causes: pain on defecation (fissure), a lump, itch or straining (haemorrhoids).
Screens for infective and upper GI causes: diarrhoea, fever, vomiting, travel or sick contacts, black tarry stools and vomiting blood.
Asks specifically about antiplatelets, anticoagulants and NSAIDs (none), and confirms metformin 1 g twice daily and Movicol one sachet daily, with no drug allergies.
check.d: Score if antiplatelets, anticoagulants and NSAIDs are asked about specifically; confirming the medicines and allergies already in the triage note is not required.

check.x: Asks about diet (low fibre) and at least one of alcohol, smoking or previous GI bleeding/abdominal surgery.
check.d: Score if diet plus one other is asked.

check.x: Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: thinks it may be piles, worried about bowel cancer, hopes to go home tonight.
Examination
Asks for the full set of vital signs and assesses for haemodynamic compromise: postural BP, peripheral perfusion (CRT) and conjunctival pallor.
check.d: Score if vital signs are asked for plus postural BP and at least one of CRT or pallor.

check.x: Examines the abdomen for tenderness, masses and organomegaly, and looks for stigmata of chronic liver disease.
Consents David for the rectal examination:

kids.x: Indication in plain words: to look for a cause of the bleeding and whether it is still bleeding
Before: undress from the waist down under a sheet, lie on the left side with knees bent
During: a look first, then one gloved, lubricated finger, asked to bear down; about a minute
Uncomfortable or an urge to open the bowels but should not hurt, and he can ask to stop at any time
Benefits and risks (quick check that guides tests; discomfort, small risk of bleeding) and alternatives (proctoscopy/sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy, which need preparation and are more invasive)
kids.d: Credit mentioning that not examining may mean slower diagnosis or more invasive tests.

kids.x: Offers a chaperone, checks understanding and gains verbal consent

check.x: Checks for contraindications (severe anal pain, local infection or an open wound) and asks about latex allergy (use non-latex gloves).
Prepares: hand hygiene and gloves, chaperone present, positions him as explained, exposed from the waist down with a sheet.
Inspects the perianal area by parting the buttocks for skin tags, fissures, haemorrhoids and masses, and asks him to strain to look for prolapse.
Warns him, inserts a lubricated finger gently with deep breaths, and assesses anal tone at rest and on squeeze.
Sweeps the rectal wall all the way round (posterior along the sacrum, both lateral walls, anterior) for masses, tenderness or stricture, and palpates the prostate.
Withdraws and inspects the glove: dark red blood and small clots mixed with brown stool, no mucus, no melaena.
Finishes: wipes him clean, covers him and helps him dress, disposes of the gloves, washes hands and tells him the findings.
Responds to the further bleed: asks for repeat observations, keeps him lying flat, and informs the registrar.
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: all in the white zone, but HR rising from 65 to 76 and SBP falling to 106 with the bleed in the ED, then settling (HR 70, SBP 112); shock index about 0.6 to 0.7 (under 1), so haemodynamically stable; notes that age can blunt the tachycardia.
check.d: Score if the rise in HR and fall in SBP with the bleed, its settling, and stability (shock index under 1 or all white zone) are stated; age blunting tachycardia is a bonus.

check.x: Identifies an acute fall in haemoglobin (124 g/L against a baseline of 141) with a normal MCV and ferritin (acute rather than chronic blood loss), and states that an early Hb underestimates the loss.

Interprets the rest of the bloods: normal platelets, INR and APTT (no coagulopathy); normal urea and creatinine (does not suggest an upper GI source); normal CRP (against infective colitis); normal LFTs; group and hold done.
check.d: Score if normal coagulation, normal urea (against upper GI) and normal CRP are interpreted.

check.x: Recognises from the report a complete colonoscopy showing diverticula with no tumour, polyp or other source, i.e. a diverticular bleed that has stopped (credit if stated to the examiner or in plain words to David).
check.d: Score if complete examination, diverticula without other source (no tumour/polyp) and bleed stopped are stated.

check.x: Gives diverticular bleeding as the most likely diagnosis, justified by at least 3 of: age over 65, chronic constipation and a low-fibre diet, sudden painless dark red blood with clots, a normal anorectal examination with blood on the glove, and normal CRP.
Gives at least 3 differentials, each with a feature for or against it from this case: colorectal cancer, angiodysplasia, haemorrhoids, anal fissure, infective colitis.
check.d: Also credit ischaemic colitis or a brisk upper GI bleed with a reason.

check.x: Management
Ensures two large-bore cannulae; group and hold done, crossmatch 2 units if further significant bleeding or deterioration; hourly observations and a stool chart.
check.d: Score if adequate IV access (two large-bore cannulae), a group and hold with a crossmatch plan for further bleeding or deterioration, and regular observations with stool or bleed monitoring are stated; ABCDE and fluid balance are not required.

check.x: Matches fluids to haemodynamics: no bolus needed while stable, or a small (250–500 mL) crystalloid bolus for postural symptoms with reassessment; maintenance fluids while fasting; restrictive transfusion threshold (Hb below 70 g/L, below 80 g/L with cardiovascular disease); no transfusion now.
check.d: Score if a fluid plan proportionate to his haemodynamics (either option) and a restrictive Hb threshold of 70 g/L with no transfusion now are stated.

check.x: Withholds metformin while he is fasting or having bowel preparation, with BGL monitoring; avoids NSAIDs; uses mechanical rather than drug VTE prophylaxis while bleeding.
Admits him (not home tonight) under gastroenterology for colonoscopy after bowel preparation on the next available list, and states that this will be explained to David because he hoped to go home.
check.d: Credit admission under general surgery if that is local practice. Also credit an Oakland score above 8 (major bleed) as the reason for admission.

check.x: States the plan if bleeding becomes brisk or he becomes unstable: escalate (registrar; rapid response for any red-zone value), crossmatch, CT angiography, then embolisation or endoscopic therapy; gastroscopy if an upper GI source is suspected.
check.d: Score if escalation plus CT angiography (with embolisation) are stated.

check.x: Explains in plain words: small pouches in the bowel wall, a small vessel at one bled and has stopped, the whole bowel was seen with no cancer or polyp, it can happen again; checks understanding.
Safety netting
Tells David the warning signs in plain words, at least 3 of: a large amount of blood or clots, feeling faint or collapsing, black tarry stools, tummy pain with fever, or breathlessness or chest pain.
Tells him to call 000 or come straight to the ED if any of these happen, rather than waiting to see his GP.

part2.lead: Here are David's observations and his blood results from the emergency department. I will give you the colonoscopy report with the last question.
part2.patient:
While the candidate answers the fourth question (explaining the colonoscopy to David), ask:

  • "So it's not cancer?" Look relieved if they explain that the whole bowel was seen and no growth or polyp was found.
  • "Will it happen again?"

If the candidate uses jargon such as "diverticula", "haematochezia" or "stigmata", ask: "What does that mean?"

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: On room air throughout. Triage set at 14:05, the nurse's repeat set after a further bleed at 14:50, and a routine set at 15:50.
handover.model:
• Read: at 14:05, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air, BP 110/75, HR 65 and temperature 37.2 °C are all in the white zone. At 14:50, after a further 100 mL of dark red blood, HR 76 and BP 106/70 (both white). By 15:50, HR 70 and BP 112/72 with no further bleeding.
  • Meaning: no value triggers a call, but the rise in HR and fall in BP with the bleed show a haemodynamic response that settled. Shock index (HR/SBP) is about 0.6 to 0.7, under 1, so he is stable. An older man's heart rate may not rise much with blood loss.
  • Changes: hourly observations with a stool chart. Any further bleed needs medical review. Escalate for a clinical review if any value enters the yellow zone and call a rapid response if any enters the red zone.

rows.note: Triage ATS 3: PR bleeding x2 at home today. IV cannula, bloods sent
Passed about 100 mL dark red blood with small clots into pan. Light-headed sitting up, settled lying down

handover.label: Blood results
handover.result: David Hughes. Collected 14:05 at cannulation. Sample not haemolysed.
handover.model:
• Read: Hb 124 g/L against a baseline of 141, with a normal MCV (89) and ferritin (145). Platelets, INR and APTT normal. Urea 6.4 and creatinine 88 normal. CRP 3 normal. LFTs normal. Glucose 8.1 (known type 2 diabetes). Group and hold done.
  • Meaning: an acute fall of about 17 g/L from a recent bleed. The normal MCV and ferritin point to acute rather than chronic loss (chronic occult loss, as from a cancer, gives iron deficiency). An early Hb underestimates the loss because haemodilution has not yet happened. No coagulopathy and no antithrombotic medicines. A normal urea does not suggest an upper GI source. Normal CRP is against infective colitis or diverticulitis. Normal LFTs and platelets, with no stigmata of chronic liver disease, make liver disease and anorectal varices unlikely. Renal function allows metformin to be restarted later.
  • Changes: no transfusion (Hb above 70 g/L); repeat the FBC in 6 to 12 hours or after any further bleed. His Oakland score is well above 8 (age, sex, blood on rectal examination, SBP and Hb 124), so this is a major bleed and he needs admission.

labs.title: Full blood count, iron and CRP
Urea, electrolytes, glucose and liver function

handover.label: Colonoscopy report
handover.result:
Examination: colonoscopy under sedation, 09:40 the morning after admission.

Clinical details: 75-year-old man. Painless dark red rectal bleeding with clots x3 yesterday. Haemodynamically stable. Hb 124 g/L (baseline 141). Type 2 diabetes, chronic constipation. No antithrombotic medicines. Rectal examination: blood on the glove, no mass.

Bowel preparation: good, with adequate views throughout.

Extent: caecum reached, confirmed by the appendiceal orifice and ileocaecal valve. Terminal ileum intubated: normal, no blood.

Findings:

  • Sigmoid and descending colon: numerous wide-mouthed diverticula (outpouchings of the colonic wall), most marked in the sigmoid. Normal haustral folds. The surrounding mucosa is pink, with no inflammation, redness, pus or mucus. No active bleeding, visible vessel or adherent clot.
  • Transverse colon, ascending colon and caecum: normal mucosa. No vascular lesions.
  • Rectum and anal canal (including retroflexion): normal. No haemorrhoids, no mass.
  • Throughout: no blood in the lumen. No polyps or masses. No angiodysplasia. No colitis. No biopsies taken.

Conclusion: extensive sigmoid and descending colon diverticulosis without inflammation or stigmata of recent haemorrhage. No other bleeding source, polyp or tumour seen. Findings consistent with a diverticular bleed that has stopped.
handover.model:
• Read: a complete examination to the caecum and terminal ileum with good preparation, so the whole colon has been seen. Multiple diverticula in the sigmoid and descending colon with normal haustral folds and no inflammation, mucus or blood. No visible vessel, clot or active bleeding. No polyp, tumour, angiodysplasia, colitis or haemorrhoids.
  • Meaning: diverticular disease (diverticulosis) is the only source found, so this is a presumed diverticular bleed that has stopped by itself. The bleeding point is rarely seen once bleeding stops. A complete, clear colonoscopy makes colorectal cancer very unlikely and makes the other differentials (angiodysplasia, colitis, haemorrhoids) unlikely. It is not diverticulitis: there is no inflammation.
  • Changes: no endoscopic treatment needed. He can go home once he is not bleeding and his Hb is stable. The candidate explains to David in plain words what the pouches are, that the bleed has stopped, that no cancer was seen, that it can recur, and the warning signs.

ask: You are now calling the gastroenterology registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of David Hughes, including your interpretation of his observations and blood results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of David now, here in the emergency department.
David had a colonoscopy the next morning; here is the report. Explain to David what it shows and what he should watch for.
expect:
• Identify: self, final-year medical student in the ED with my supervising registrar; David Hughes, 75.
  • Situation: painless fresh rectal bleeding today with an Hb fall, currently stable; requesting admission and colonoscopy.
  • Background: two bleeds at home, dark red with clots, one more of 100 mL in the ED; no pain, no change in bowel habit or weight loss; T2DM on metformin, chronic constipation on Movicol; no antithrombotics or NSAIDs; FOBT negative 2 years ago.
  • Assessment: obs white zone; HR 65 to 76 and SBP 106 with the ED bleed, settled; shock index under 1. PR: blood and clots, no mass or anorectal cause. Hb 124 (baseline 141), normocytic, normal ferritin: acute loss; normal coagulation, urea and CRP; group and hold done. Likely diverticular bleed.
  • Recommendation: please review for admission and colonoscopy after bowel prep.

Diverticular bleeding: age 75, chronic constipation, low-fibre diet, sudden painless large-volume dark red blood with clots, normal anorectal examination, normal CRP.

  • Colorectal cancer (must not miss): for: age, constipation; against: stable bowel habit, no weight loss, no rectal mass, normal ferritin (a negative screening FOBT 2 years ago gives little reassurance in a symptomatic patient).
  • Angiodysplasia: for: over 60, painless; against: no murmur to suggest aortic stenosis, normal renal function, normal ferritin with no previous bleeding; large dark clots fit a diverticular bleed better.
  • Haemorrhoids: for: straining; against: no lump or itch, clots mixed with stool, normal inspection.
  • Anal fissure: for: constipation; against: painless, no fissure seen.
  • Infective colitis: against: no diarrhoea, fever or travel, CRP 3.

1. ABCDE; two large-bore cannulae; bloods sent; group and hold done; crossmatch 2 units if there is further significant bleeding or haemodynamic deterioration; hourly observations, stool chart, fluid balance.
  2. Fluids matched to haemodynamics: no bolus needed while stable, or a small (250–500 mL) crystalloid bolus for postural symptoms with reassessment; maintenance fluids while fasting; restrictive transfusion threshold (Hb below 70 g/L, below 80 g/L with cardiovascular disease); no transfusion now; repeat FBC.
  3. Withhold metformin while fasting or on bowel prep, BGL monitoring; no NSAIDs; mechanical VTE prophylaxis.
  4. Admit under gastroenterology for colonoscopy after bowel prep on the next available list; this will be explained to David, who hoped to go home tonight.
  5. If brisk bleeding or unstable: escalate (rapid response for red zone), crossmatch, CT angiography, then embolisation or endoscopic therapy; gastroscopy if an upper GI source is suspected.

• Plain words: small pouches in the bowel wall; most likely a small blood vessel at one of the pouches bled and has stopped; the whole bowel was seen and there is no cancer or polyp; it can happen again; checks understanding.
  • Red flags: call 000 or come to the ED for heavy bleeding or clots, feeling faint, black stools, tummy pain with fever.

ddx.for: A 75-year-old with lifelong constipation and a low-fibre diet who suddenly passed a large volume of painless dark red blood with clots, has a normal anorectal examination and CRP, and whose colonoscopy shows extensive sigmoid and descending diverticula with no other source.
He is 75 with chronic constipation and has never had a colonoscopy.
ddx.against: No change in bowel habit, weight loss or tiredness, no rectal mass, normal MCV and ferritin, and no tumour or polyp on a complete colonoscopy (a negative screening FOBT 2 years ago gives little reassurance in a symptomatic patient).

ddx.for: He is over 60 and the bleeding was painless.
ddx.against: No vascular lesions were seen on a complete colonoscopy and diverticula explain the bleed.

ddx.for: Years of constipation with straining when he forgets his Movicol.
ddx.against: No lump, itch or prolapse, the blood was dark with clots and mixed with stool rather than on the paper, and no haemorrhoids on inspection or retroflexion.
The bleeding was painless, with no pain on opening the bowels, and no fissure was seen on inspection.
No diarrhoea, fever, vomiting, travel or sick contacts, CRP 3, and normal mucosa on colonoscopy.

guide:
This station focuses on consent and the rectal examination, so the history should be focused: about 3 to 4 minutes on the bleed, its effects and the red flags. The triage note in the stem already gives the past history, medicines and FOBT. If there is no manikin, the candidate describes each step of the examination aloud and the examiner gives the findings from the Exam findings. David asks "Will it hurt?" and "Do you really need to do it?" during consent. Credit consent only if the candidate offers a chaperone and David agrees before the examination starts. The nurse reports the further bleed at the 8-minute mark, or as soon as the rectal examination is finished if that is earlier. If the candidate orders treatment, say "Noted, please cover it in Part 2". If they ask for results, say these come in Part 2.

In Part 2, hand over the observations and bloods and ask the first three questions in order. Hand over the colonoscopy report with the fourth question. David's questions are put during the fourth answer.

A high-performing candidate characterises the bleed (painless, dark red with clots, large volume), asks about light-headedness, cancer red flags and antithrombotics, and checks the postural BP. They give a clear consent with indication, procedure, the right to stop, risks, alternatives and a chaperone, then examine systematically and inspect the glove. In Part 2 they recognise an acute Hb fall with stable haemodynamics, admit for colonoscopy rather than sending him home, know when CT angiography is needed, read the colonoscopy as a diverticular bleed with no cancer and safety-net clearly.

A borderline candidate starts the examination without proper consent or a chaperone, forgets to look at the glove, misses the antithrombotic question, or plans discharge tonight. A candidate who performs the examination without gaining consent should not pass the consent item.
explain:
Diagnosis: diverticular bleeding

David is 75, has had chronic constipation for years and eats a low-fibre diet. He suddenly passed a large volume of painless dark red blood with clots, then bled once more in the ED. He stayed haemodynamically stable and the bleeding settled. His anorectal examination was normal apart from blood on the glove, and a complete colonoscopy showed extensive sigmoid and descending colon diverticula with no other source. This is a diverticular bleed that has stopped.

Diverticula are mucosal outpouchings through weak points in the colon wall where blood vessels enter. They are common after 65, especially with constipation and a low-fibre diet. The artery stretched over a diverticulum can rupture and bleed. This is typically sudden, painless and large-volume, bright red or maroon with clots, and usually stops by itself, though it can recur. NSAIDs, antiplatelets and anticoagulants increase the risk. Diverticular bleeding is not the same as diverticulitis: diverticulitis gives left iliac fossa pain and fever, is diagnosed with CT, and colonoscopy is avoided during an acute attack.

Consent and the rectal examination

  • Consent: explain why (to look for a structural cause and for active bleeding), what happens before (undress from the waist down, left lateral position with the knees bent, a chaperone, ideally a staff member such as a nurse (a family member may be present for support if he wishes)), during (inspection, one gloved lubricated finger, bearing down, a sweep of the rectum, about a minute; it may be uncomfortable or feel like needing to go, but should not hurt, and he can stop at any time) and after (get dressed, then discuss the findings). Give benefits, risks (discomfort, small risk of bleeding, very small risk of infection, latex allergy) and the consequences of not doing it (slower diagnosis, more invasive tests). Alternatives are colonoscopy or rigid sigmoidoscopy, which need preparation and are more invasive. Check understanding in chunks, in plain language, and gain verbal consent.
  • Contraindications: extreme pain, local inflammation or infection, and an open wound.
  • Examination: hand hygiene and gloves, chaperone, left lateral position, sheet before and after. Inspect for skin tags, fissures, haemorrhoids and masses, and ask him to strain for prolapse. Warn him, ask for deep breaths and enter gently. Assess tone at rest and on squeeze. Sweep the posterior wall along the sacrum, both lateral walls and the anterior wall (prostate in men) for tenderness, stricture or masses. Inspect the glove for stool colour, blood and mucus. Clean him, help him dress, dispose of the gloves and wash your hands.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: all in the white zone, with a small, settling rise in HR and fall in BP with the ED bleed. A shock index (HR/SBP) under 1 means he is stable. Older patients may not mount a tachycardia, so trends matter.
  • Bloods: an acute Hb fall from 141 to 124 g/L with a normal MCV and ferritin means acute, not chronic, blood loss. The first Hb underestimates the loss. Normal coagulation, a normal urea (a raised urea suggests an upper GI source), a normal CRP and normal LFTs narrow the differentials.
  • Colonoscopy: the bleeding point in a diverticular bleed is rarely seen once it stops, so the diagnosis rests on finding diverticula and no other source on a complete examination. A clear, complete colonoscopy makes colorectal cancer very unlikely.

Differentials for fresh rectal bleeding

  • Colorectal cancer: change in bowel habit, weight loss, fatigue, iron deficiency, family history, smoking and alcohol. Investigated with FOBT (screening), colonoscopy and CT staging; treated by stage with polypectomy, resection, radiotherapy or palliation. FOBT is a screening test and should not be used to investigate symptomatic bleeding; symptomatic patients need colonoscopy.
  • Haemorrhoids: vascular cushions. Internal ones are painless and external haemorrhoids are painful when thrombosed, with a lump or itch, from straining (constipation, pregnancy, lifting). Portal hypertension causes anorectal varices, which are distinct from haemorrhoids. A clinical diagnosis; treated with fibre, softeners and sitz baths, then banding or haemorrhoidectomy.
  • Anal fissure: a tear in the lining of the distal anal canal (anoderm) below the dentate line, with severe pain on defecation. Treated with fibre, softeners, sitz baths and topical GTN or a calcium channel blocker, then botulinum toxin or sphincterotomy.
  • Angiodysplasia: vascular malformations in people over 60, causing painless episodes; watch for anaemia.
  • Infective colitis: pain, diarrhoea, vomiting, fever, travel or contacts. Send stool MCS; give fluids, and antibiotics if severe or immunocompromised; avoid antibiotics if Shiga toxin-producing E. coli is suspected (risk of haemolytic uraemic syndrome). Bloody diarrhoea suggests Campylobacter, haemorrhagic E. coli, Entamoeba, Shigella, Salmonella or Yersinia.
  • Ischaemic colitis and a brisk upper GI bleed are also worth considering in an older patient.

Investigations

FBC, UEC, LFTs, CRP, coagulation and a group and hold (crossmatch for ongoing bleeding); stool MCS if there is diarrhoea; colonoscopy; and CT, as CT angiography if the bleeding is brisk.

Management

The British Society of Gastroenterology guideline on acute lower GI bleeding is a useful framework:

  • Unstable (shock index above 1 after resuscitation): CT angiography to find the bleeding point, then catheter angiography and embolisation; consider gastroscopy because an upper GI source can present this way. Surgery is a last resort.
  • Stable, major bleed (Oakland score above 8): admit for colonoscopy on the next available list. David's age (2), male sex (1), blood on rectal examination (1), heart rate (0 to 1), systolic BP 106 to 110 (4) and Hb 124 g/L (8) give a score of about 16, well above 8.
  • Stable, minor bleed (Oakland score 8 or less): can be discharged for outpatient investigation.
  • Transfusion: restrictive, with a threshold of Hb 70 g/L (80 g/L with cardiovascular disease), as the BSG guideline and the National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management guidelines support.
  • Medicines: withhold metformin while fasting or on bowel preparation and monitor glucose; avoid NSAIDs; use mechanical VTE prophylaxis while bleeding.

Long-term management of diverticular disease is fibre, fluids, mobility and laxatives to avoid constipation. Surgery is kept for complications such as abscess or fistula, or recurrent severe bleeding.

Safety netting

David can go home once he has stopped bleeding and his Hb is stable. He should call 000 or come straight to the ED for heavy bleeding or clots, feeling faint, black stools, or tummy pain with fever. He restarts metformin once he is eating normally after the colonoscopy and sees his GP within 1 to 2 weeks for a repeat FBC. He should keep taking Movicol, increase fibre and fluids, keep active and avoid anti-inflammatories.
points: Diverticular bleeding is sudden, painless and often large-volume, bright red or maroon with clots, in an older patient with constipation or a low-fibre diet. It usually stops by itself but can recur.

Consent for a rectal examination covers the indication, what happens before, during and after, that it should not hurt and can be stopped at any time, the risks, the alternatives and a chaperone, followed by verbal consent.
Examine systematically: inspect and ask him to strain, check tone at rest and on squeeze, sweep the whole rectal wall and the prostate, then always inspect the glove.
Risk-stratify a lower GI bleed with the observations, shock index, haemoglobin trend and antithrombotic use. The first Hb underestimates the loss, and older patients may not become tachycardic.
Stable major bleeds are admitted for colonoscopy after bowel preparation. Unstable bleeding needs resuscitation, CT angiography and embolisation, with gastroscopy considered for an upper GI source.
Use a restrictive transfusion threshold (Hb 70 g/L, or 80 g/L with cardiovascular disease). Withhold metformin during fasting and bowel preparation, and avoid NSAIDs.
